![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14210206/assets/740d181b8e8eff44f0eb258c8b68f30d05f70445aefabd5c00fd68e570e825dd.png)

The sides of a square are increasing in length at a rate of $3\text{ mm/s}.$ At what rate is the area of the square changing when the sides have a length of $12\text{ mm}?$
q-24800.worked_solution:
Let $x$ and $A$ be the length of the sides and the area of the square, respectively. We want to find

$$
\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}.
$$

The area $A$ is related to side length $x$ by the formula

$$
A={x}^{2}.
$$

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({x}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot 2x\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that each side of the square is increasing at a rate of $3\,\text{mm/s},$ so we have $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=3.$ Also, when the sides are $12\,\text{mm},$ we have $x=12.$ Substituting this information into the above, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =3\cdot 2(12)=72{\text{ mm}}^{2}\text{/s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the area of the square increases at $72\,{\text{mm}}^{2}/\text{s}.$

Question 1

The sides of a square are increasing in length at a rate of 3 mm/s. At what rate is the area of the square changing when the sides have a length of 12 mm?

a

b
36 mm2/s
c
8 mm2/s
d
24 mm2/s
e
72 mm2/s

EXPLANATION

Let x and A be the length of the sides and the area of the square, respectively. We want to find

dAdt.

The area A is related to side length x by the formula

A=x2.

Differentiating this relationship with respect to t using implicit differentiation, we get

ddt(A)=ddt(x2)dAdt=dxdt⋅ddx(x2)dAdt=dxdt⋅2x

We're told that each side of the square is increasing at a rate of 3mm/s, so we have dxdt=3. Also, when the sides are 12mm, we have x=12. Substituting this information into the above, we get

dAdt=3⋅2(12)=72 mm2/s.

Therefore, the area of the square increases at 72mm2/s.

The sides (in meters) of a square are decreasing. At a particular moment, the rate of decrease of the area of the square is numerically equal to ten times the rate of decrease of the sides. What is the length of the sides of the square at that moment?

a
2 m
b
10 m
c
5 m
d
2.5 m
e
12 m
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Let x and A be the length of the sides and the area of the square, respectively. We want to find

dAdt.

The area A is related to side length x by the formula

A=x2.

Differentiating this relationship with respect to t using implicit differentiation, we get

ddt(A)=ddt(x2)dAdt=dxdt⋅ddx(x2)dAdt=dxdt⋅2x

The given information tells us that dAdt=10⋅dxdt. So, substituting dAdt in the above gives

10⋅dxdt=2x⋅dxdt10⋅dxdt=2x⋅dxdt10=2xx=5.

Therefore, at that particular moment we have x=5 m.

The sides of a square are increasing in length at a rate of $8\text{ ft/s}.$ At what rate is the area of ​​the square increasing when the side is $4\,\text{ft}$ long?

The area is increasing at a rate of
{{field-1}} ${\text{ft}}^{2}/\text{s}.$
q-314491.worked_solution:
Let $x$ and $A$ be the length of the sides and the area of the square, respectively. We want to find

$$
\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}.
$$

The area $A$ is related to side length $x$ by the formula

$$
A={x}^{2}.
$$

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({x}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot 2x\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that each side of the square is increasing at a rate of $8\,\text{ft/s},$ so we have $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=8.$ Also, when the sides are $4\,\text{ft},$ we have $x=4.$ Substituting this information into the above, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =8\cdot 2(4) \\  & =64{\text{ ft}}^{2}\text{/s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the area of the square increases at $64\,{\text{ft}}^{2}/\text{s}.$

A=\frac{{h}^{2}}{2}.
$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}4\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} & =h\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} \\ 4\cancel{\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}} & =h\cancel{\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}} \\ 4 & =h.\end{aligned}

$$

$$

$$

Therefore, the perimeter of the square increases at $16\text{ feet}/\text{hour}.$

$$
A=\frac{{h}^{2}}{2}.

$$
\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}.

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} & =-2.\end{aligned}

$$
